stages.title: Advanced physical geography
stages.hook: Glaciers, deserts, coasts and soils look unrelated. What do they have in common as shapers of land?
explain: Physical geography studies how Earth's surface is shaped by the lithosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere acting together. Landscapes result from a balance between uplift and building processes, and wearing-down processes.

Glaciers form where more snow falls than melts, compressing into ice that flows downhill under gravity. They carve U-shaped valleys, cirques and arêtes, and deposit moraines. About 10 percent of land is covered by ice, mostly in Antarctica and Greenland, holding roughly 69 percent of Earth's fresh water.

Deserts are defined by low precipitation (usually under 250 mm a year), not by heat. Wind moves sand into dunes, but most desert landforms are shaped by rare flash floods. Coasts are shaped by waves: erosion makes cliffs, caves, arches and stacks, while deposition forms beaches, spits and bars.

Soil forms slowly from weathered rock, organic matter, water and air, influenced by climate, organisms, relief and time. A soil profile has horizons: O (organic), A (topsoil), B (subsoil) and C (weathered rock). Poor land use causes degradation through erosion, salinisation and loss of nutrients.

example.q: A desert gets 180 mm of rain a year. Under the common 250 mm rule, is it a desert, and does it need to be hot?
steps: 180 mm is below 250 mm, so it meets the low-rainfall rule.
Deserts are defined by dryness, not temperature.
Cold places such as Antarctica also count.
example.a: Yes it is a desert; heat is not required

analogies.home: A tap dripping onto a bar of soap carves a channel slowly, like water on rock.
analogies.farm: Farmers plant cover crops and terraces to keep soil from washing or blowing away.
analogies.sea: Waves undercut cliffs the way a saw cuts under a plank.
analogies.nature: A glacier is like a slow conveyor belt for rock.

stages.mnemonic: Glaciers gouge, waves wear, winds winnow, soils slowly grow.

misc.wrong: Wind is the main cause of landforms in deserts.
misc.right: Wind moves sand, but occasional running water shapes many desert valleys and fans.

stages.limits: Rates of change vary greatly, from slow rock weathering to sudden landslides, so landscapes reflect past climates as well as present ones.

stages.title: Climate systems and variability
stages.hook: Why does the Pacific Ocean decide whether Peru floods and Australia burns in some years?
explain: Climate is the statistical pattern of weather over at least about 30 years. The climate system includes the atmosphere, oceans, ice, land surface and living things. The greenhouse effect warms Earth: gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane absorb outgoing infrared radiation and re-emit some of it downward. Without it Earth's average temperature would be around −18 °C instead of about +15 °C.
Albedo is the fraction of sunlight reflected. Fresh snow reflects most; dark ocean absorbs most. Changes in ice cover can therefore amplify temperature changes (a positive feedback).

Climate varies naturally. The El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is a swing in the tropical Pacific. In El Niño, trade winds weaken and warm water spreads east, bringing floods to coastal Peru and often drought to Australia and Indonesia. La Niña has the opposite pattern. Cycles come every 2 to 7 years.

Other patterns include the monsoon (seasonal reversal of winds driven by land-sea heating differences) and the North Atlantic Oscillation, which affects European winters. Temperature falls with height at about 6.5 °C per km (the average environmental lapse rate).

example.q: A town at sea level has an average temperature of 20 °C. Estimate the temperature of a village 2,000 m higher, using 6.5 °C per km.

analogies.home: A car parked in sunlight heats up because glass lets sunlight in but slows heat getting out, like greenhouse gases.
analogies.sea: Warm and cool ocean patches change rain over land far away.
analogies.farm: Farmers watch ENSO forecasts to choose crops and plan water.
analogies.tech: Computer models simulate the atmosphere and oceans to forecast climate patterns.

stages.mnemonic: Greenhouse traps heat; albedo bounces light; ENSO swings the Pacific.
terms: Warming of Earth because some gases absorb and re-emit heat.

misc.wrong: The greenhouse effect is the same as global warming.
misc.right: The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth habitable. Global warming is the extra warming from rising greenhouse gases.

stages.limits: ENSO strength and timing are hard to forecast far ahead, and its links to climate change are active research.

stages.title: Hydrology and watershed management
stages.hook: Two catchments get the same storm. One floods in an hour and the other barely rises. What differs?
explain: Hydrology studies the movement and storage of water. A catchment (drainage basin) is the land that drains to a river. Inputs are precipitation; outputs are evaporation, transpiration and river flow; stores include vegetation, soil, groundwater and lakes.

Water reaches rivers by overland flow, throughflow in soil and groundwater flow. Infiltration is soil absorption; it falls when the ground is saturated, frozen, paved or steeply sloped. Impermeable surfaces send water quickly to rivers, giving a short lag time and a high peak discharge.

Discharge is the volume passing a point per unit time: Q = A × v (cross-section area times mean velocity), in m³/s. A storm hydrograph plots discharge against time. A flashy hydrograph has a steep rising limb and a high, early peak; a gentle one is typical of forested, permeable catchments.

Management combines hard engineering (dams, levees, channels) and soft approaches (afforestation, wetlands, floodplain zoning, flood warnings). Dams can store water and make electricity but alter sediment, ecology and people's lives. Rivers crossing borders need shared governance.

example.q: A river channel is 20 m wide and 2 m deep on average with a mean velocity of 1.5 m/s. What is the discharge?

analogies.home: A sponge soaks up spilled water, but a plate lets it run off, like permeable and impermeable ground.
analogies.city: Paved streets and drains send rain quickly to rivers; green roofs and rain gardens slow it.
analogies.farm: Terraces and ponds hold water on fields and recharge groundwater.
analogies.tech: River gauges and satellites feed flood warning systems.

misc.wrong: Building a dam always reduces flood risk for everyone.

stages.limits: Hydrological models rely on gauge data that is sparse in many regions, so predictions carry uncertainty.

stages.title: Geomorphology
stages.hook: The Himalaya rise about 5 mm a year yet erode quickly. How can a mountain grow and wear away at the same time?
explain: Geomorphology studies landforms and the processes that shape them. Endogenic (internal) processes such as tectonic uplift and volcanism build relief. Exogenic (external) processes such as weathering, erosion, transport and deposition lower it. Relief is the balance of both over time.

Weathering breaks rock down in place. Physical weathering includes freeze-thaw, where water freezes in cracks and expands about 9 percent. Chemical weathering changes minerals, for example carbonic acid dissolving limestone to make caves and karst. Biological weathering involves roots and organisms.
Mass movement is downslope movement under gravity, from slow creep to rapid landslides, often triggered by heavy rain or earthquakes. Slopes fail when driving forces exceed resistance.

Different rocks make different landscapes: resistant granite forms uplands; limestone gives karst with sinkholes; sandstone forms cliffs. Landscapes are also inherited from past climates. Much of northern Europe and North America was shaped by ice sheets during the last ice age, which ended about 11,700 years ago.

example.q: A mountain is uplifted at 4 mm per year and eroded at 3 mm per year. What is the net change in height per year, and after 1 million years?
example.a: +1 mm a year, about +1,000 m in a million years

analogies.home: Sandcastles slump when too wet, like slopes failing after heavy rain.
analogies.farm: Terraces stop soil creep on steep fields.
analogies.city: Hillside cities use retaining walls and drains to prevent landslides.

misc.right: Mountains rise and are worn down over millions of years; relief reflects ongoing balance.

stages.title: Economic geography
stages.hook: Two countries have the same total income, yet life in one seems far better. How do we measure development fairly?
explain: Economic geography studies where economic activity occurs and why. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) measures the value of goods and services produced in a country in a year. GDP per capita divides GDP by population. It is a rough indicator of average income but hides inequality and unpaid work.

The Human Development Index (HDI) combines life expectancy, education and income per person into a number between 0 and 1. Other indicators are infant mortality, literacy and access to clean water. Countries are often grouped by income or HDI, but classification systems change.

Trade links regions. Comparative advantage means a country gains by specialising in what it produces at lower opportunity cost. Raw materials often sell for less than manufactured goods, so exporting only raw materials can leave countries vulnerable to price swings.

Development differs across space. Core-periphery models describe rich cores with strong industry and services and poorer peripheries, at scales from cities to continents. Globalisation links economies through trade, investment, migration and information, with gains for many but also inequality and dislocation.

example.q: A country has a GDP of 600 billion dollars and 50 million people. What is GDP per capita?

analogies.home: Family income per person tells you more than total income in a big household.
analogies.city: Cities often have the highest incomes but also big gaps between rich and poor.
analogies.farm: A country that exports only raw crops depends on weather and global prices.
analogies.tech: Digital services allow some countries to jump into high-value work.

misc.wrong: A high GDP means everyone is well off.
misc.right: GDP is a total or an average; it can hide wide inequality and says nothing about health or the environment.

stages.limits: Development indices simplify complex realities, and different measures rank countries differently.

stages.title: Political geography and borders
stages.hook: A line on a map can mean peace, a dispute or a closed gate. What makes a border real?
explain: A state is a political unit with defined territory, a permanent population, a government and recognised sovereignty. A nation is a group sharing identity, such as language, culture or history. Nation-states try to match the two, but many states contain several nations and some nations are spread across several states, such as the Kurds or the Sámi.

Boundaries can follow physical features (rivers, mountains), geometric lines (straight lines of latitude or longitude, as in parts of the United States–Canada border and in Africa) or cultural features (language, religion). Many African boundaries were drawn in the 1880s by European powers at the Berlin Conference, often without regard for local societies.

Under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, coastal states have territorial seas to 12 nautical miles and an Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) of up to 200 nautical miles for resources. One nautical mile is 1.852 km.

Some borders are disputed. Geographers describe such cases neutrally, noting who claims what, and how maps differ. Supranational organisations such as the European Union and African Union show how states may share some decisions. Geopolitics studies how geography influences power and international relations.

example.q: A coastal state's EEZ extends 200 nautical miles. Convert to kilometres (1 nautical mile = 1.852 km).

analogies.home: Fences between gardens show who is responsible for each, but neighbours can disagree about where they lie.
analogies.sea: Fishing rights depend on the EEZ boundaries.
analogies.city: Even cities have boundaries that decide taxes and services.
analogies.tech: Satellite imagery is used to map and verify borders.

stages.mnemonic: State is the land and government, nation is the people who share identity.
terms: Supreme authority of a state over its territory.

stages.limits: Disputed territories exist worldwide, and different governments and maps may show them differently. Geographers present the claims rather than choose.

stages.title: Transport and logistics geography
stages.hook: A T-shirt may travel across three continents before you wear it. How does it move so cheaply?
explain: Transport geography studies how people and goods move. Modes are road, rail, water, air and pipeline. Each balances cost, speed, capacity and flexibility. Sea transport is slow but very cheap per tonne; air freight is fast but costly; road gives door-to-door flexibility; rail suits heavy bulk on land.

The standardised shipping container, widely adopted from the 1960s, cut handling costs and let goods switch between ship, train and truck (intermodal transport). Most of the world's traded goods by volume travel by sea.

Networks use nodes (ports, airports, stations) and links (routes). A hub-and-spoke system routes traffic through a central hub to many smaller spokes, which saves routes but concentrates traffic. Just-in-time logistics keeps stocks low but is sensitive to delays.

Chokepoints are narrow passages where traffic concentrates: the Suez Canal (opened 1869), the Panama Canal (opened 1914), the Strait of Malacca and the Strait of Hormuz. Blocking one raises costs. Distance is not just kilometres; time and cost matter, so geographers also use friction of distance.

example.q: A ship sails at 20 knots. One knot is 1 nautical mile per hour (1.852 km/h). How long to sail 3,000 nautical miles?

analogies.home: A neighbourhood shop is a spoke; the supermarket warehouse is the hub.
analogies.city: Bus and metro networks use interchange stations as nodes.
analogies.farm: Refrigerated trucks and containers carry fruit across oceans.
analogies.sea: Ports with deep water and cranes handle the biggest ships.

stages.mnemonic: Nodes and links, hubs and spokes, boxes on boats.
terms: Moving goods in one container by more than one mode.
A network where routes pass through a central hub.

How cost and time reduce movement with distance.

misc.wrong: Air freight carries most world trade.
misc.right: Most trade by volume goes by sea; air carries a small share of high-value, urgent goods.

stages.limits: Trade statistics differ by whether weight or value is counted. By value, air carries a larger share.

teach.model: Goods move by road, rail, sea, air and pipeline, each with its own cost and speed. Containers make switching modes easy. Networks of hubs and chokepoints decide how efficient, and how fragile, trade is.

stages.title: Geographic information systems
stages.hook: A map app can show traffic, weather and shops all at once. How is that possible from a flat screen?
explain: A Geographic Information System (GIS) stores, analyses and displays spatial data. Data are organised into layers, each holding one theme such as roads, rivers, land use or elevation. Layers share a coordinate system so they overlay precisely.

There are two data models. Vector data uses points (a well), lines (a road) and polygons (a lake) with attribute tables. Raster data is a grid of cells, each with a value, such as elevation or satellite pixels. Resolution is the cell size.

Maps flatten a sphere, so projections distort something: area, shape, distance or direction. The Mercator projection preserves shape and compass bearings locally, which suits navigation, but exaggerates areas near the poles (Greenland looks as big as Africa, though Africa is about 14 times larger). Equal-area projections keep sizes true.

GIS operations include buffering (zones around features), overlay (combining layers) and querying. A planner can find sites within 500 m of a road and outside a flood zone. GNSS/GPS gives positions from satellites with several metres of accuracy.

example.q: A raster map has cells of 30 m by 30 m. How many hectares does one cell cover? (1 hectare = 10,000 m²)

analogies.home: Transparent sheets stacked on a table, each with one drawing, are like GIS layers.
analogies.city: Planners overlay schools, bus routes and population to find who lacks access.
analogies.farm: Farmers map soil and yield layers to apply fertiliser only where needed.
analogies.sea: Marine GIS shows depth, currents and shipping lanes.

stages.mnemonic: Layers stack, vectors draw, rasters grid.
terms: A system for storing, analysing and mapping spatial data.
Points, lines and polygons with attributes.
A grid of cells with values.
A method of flattening the globe onto a map.

misc.wrong: A map projection can show shapes, areas and distances all perfectly.
misc.right: Every flat projection distorts at least one property of the globe.

stages.limits: GIS results depend on data quality, scale and the choices the analyst makes.

teach.model: A GIS stacks layers of spatial data in a common coordinate system. Vector data uses points, lines and polygons; raster data uses grids. Projections flatten the globe and always distort something.

stages.title: Remote sensing and satellite mapping
stages.hook: A satellite can tell how green a forest is without anyone going there. How?
explain: Remote sensing collects information about Earth from a distance, usually with sensors on satellites, aircraft or drones. Passive sensors record reflected sunlight or emitted heat; active sensors, such as radar and lidar, send their own signal and record the return.

Different surfaces reflect and emit different wavelengths. Healthy plants absorb red light for photosynthesis and reflect a lot of near-infrared. The Normalised Difference Vegetation Index is NDVI = (NIR − Red) ÷ (NIR + Red). Values near 1 show dense healthy vegetation; near 0 bare ground; negative values water or snow.

Resolution has four forms: spatial (pixel size), spectral (number of bands), temporal (how often a place is revisited) and radiometric (sensitivity). Landsat satellites have imaged the whole Earth since 1972 with 30 m pixels, giving a long record of change. Radar can see through clouds and at night.

Uses include mapping land cover, tracking deforestation, monitoring floods and droughts, measuring sea ice and guiding disaster response. Images are checked against ground truth, direct observations in the field.

example.q: A pixel reflects near-infrared 0.50 and red 0.10. Calculate NDVI.

analogies.home: A camera sees colours; a thermal camera sees heat. Satellites carry sensors for many invisible kinds of light.
analogies.farm: Farmers use NDVI images to find stressed crops.
analogies.city: Night-time light images show where cities and power are.
analogies.sea: Satellites track sea-surface temperature and sea ice.

stages.mnemonic: Sensors see what eyes cannot: red, near-infrared, heat and radar.
terms: Gathering information about Earth from a distance.
An index of vegetation greenness from red and near-infrared light.
The size of the smallest ground detail a pixel can show.
Field observations used to check images.

misc.right: Many sensors record invisible wavelengths or radar signals, and images are processed and calibrated before use.

stages.limits: Clouds, shadows and mixed pixels can mislead classification, so results need checking.
